Moscow Principality. Also known as the Grand Principality of Moscow, this medieval Russian state emerged from fragmented territories under Mongol rule and grew into the nucleus of the Russian Empire. From a minor settlement in the twelfth century, Moscow rose to dominance through strategic location, diplomatic maneuvering, and military conquest, ultimately unifying the Russian lands and throwing off foreign control. Prince Yuri Dolgoruki founded Moscow as a small fortified settlement in the twelfth century, situated at the intersection of major trade routes and surrounded by forests offering defensive advantages. The principality rose to prominence in the fourteenth century under Ivan I, also called Ivan Moneybag, who secured the title of Grand Prince and established Moscow as the seat of the Russian Orthodox Church's metropolitan, giving it religious authority as well as political power. The transformation accelerated under Ivan III, known as the Gatherer of Lands, who ruled from 1462 to 1505 and dramatically expanded Moscow's power by subduing rival principalities, throwing off Mongol overlordship, and establishing Moscow's hegemony over Russian territories. Most notably, Ivan III defeated the Golden Horde, the Mongol state that had dominated Russian territories for over two centuries, declaring independence and establishing Moscow as the leader of Russian liberation. Ivan IV, known as Ivan the Terrible and ruling from 1530 to 1584, further transformed the Moscow Principality into the Russian Tsardom by conquering additional territories and centralizing autocratic power. The principality's rulers adopted Byzantine imperial symbols and married into Byzantine royalty, positioning Moscow as the heir to Constantinople's legacy and claiming the status of Third Rome. This sophisticated state developed bureaucratic structures, military institutions, and cultural achievements that established the foundation for the Russian Empire's later rise to great-power status.
